beats.trigger: ## Lecture: Grounded, and four candidates to measure
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: When your sources support a request, the output is grounded. When they don't, the agent still produces something, and the tone looks the same.
beats.got: The thing sounds equally sure whether or not it has a source. That is a fair point about confident juniors too.

beats.trigger: Ten unverified steps in a row (retrieval, synthesis, formatting, writing, checking, rewriting, summarising, publishing) at 85% each come to about 20% end-to-end
beats.got: Small error rates multiply across a chain, so an unchecked workflow is mostly wrong. I can check that arithmetic myself, which I like.
Tidy numbers on an assumed 90% catch rate. Looks like a sales slide, even though it says 'say'.

beats.trigger: Later models may fabricate less; the mechanism stays the same.
beats.got: Asking the model to double-check itself is worthless, and they admit newer models won't fix the mechanism. Candid, and I can try it in thirty seconds.

beats.trigger: You don't know which detection method catches what matters on *your* output, on *your* strategic question.
beats.got: Don't trust the vendor's recommended check. Test several on my own material. That is the opposite of the last programmes.

beats.trigger: **3. Citation integrity.** When the briefing cites a source, does the source contain the claim? Catches *citation cargo-cult*.
beats.got: Four checks, each aimed at a different failure: invention, overreach, fake citation, contradiction. Reasonable taxonomy, a bit jargon-heavy.

beats.trigger: Citation integrity caught a quote absent from the linked sanctions order.
beats.got: A real case with specific catches that differ by method. First concrete evidence that the four checks find different things.

beats.trigger: Grounded output names what it doesn't know. A grounded judge names what it can't catch.
beats.got: The saved check has to state where it stops working. Honest design, though 'judge file' is just a prompt.

beats.trigger: Grounding is the discipline; fabrication is the failure: invented case law, invented medications, confident numbers nobody can source.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Two runs is a demo, not a measurement.
beats.got: Stable answers can still be wrong, and two runs prove nothing. A course admitting its own demo is weak is rare.

beats.trigger: Run all four on your own output and keep the one that caught what mattered.
beats.got: I set up a test, agents run it, I read a scoreboard. Fifty-five minutes is a lot, though.

beats.trigger: Aim for roughly 10% fabrication or misrepresentation: enough wrongness for the detectors to have a job, not nonsense.
beats.got: We make the AI lie on purpose so we can test the checkers. Clever, but it's a lab setup, not my real work.

beats.trigger: Why a separate worker? It runs in its own context, so your main session never sees what was fabricated.
beats.got: The fakes are kept hidden from me so the test is fair. Sensible.

beats.trigger: The scoreboard IS the explanation. You can point at a row and say *this is why I'm keeping this one*.

take_homes: Chained steps compound errors: ten steps at 85% each is about 20% correct. Without a check, most of the output has a defect.
Don't believe the model when it says it's sure. Test several checks on my own material and read which one catches what.
Judge the check by a scoreboard I can argue with, and make it state its own blind spots.

misconception.why: I came expecting recycled slides. The Mata v. Avianca catches by method, the 85% arithmetic and the admission that 'Two runs is a demo, not a measurement' were concrete and checkable. It's a testing method, not a transformation, so it does not change my view of the wider wave. Wait-and-see on the big claims still stands.

one_line: Less slideware than I expected: a way to measure whether the AI is making things up, and it admits what it can't catch. I still don't know if it matters at my level.
